claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Sánchez Alvarado and Newmark, 1999 and Pineda et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Planarian triclad flatworm photoreceptors express conserved members of the r-opsin signaling cascade (e.g. Gαq, Trp channel-encoding genes).
claims.source: Their eyes typically consist of photoreceptors with rhabdomes of microvilli that are associated with pigmented shading cells (Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001) and which, in planarian triclad flatworms, have been shown to express rhabdomeric opsin (Sánchez Alvarado and Newmark, 1999; Pineda et al., 2000) and conserved members of the r-opsin signaling cascade (e.g. Gαq, Trp channel-encoding genes) (Lapan and Reddien, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Lapan and Reddien, 2012.

claims.claim: Xenopsins but not c-opsins have been described in flatworms.
claims.source: The presence and nature of ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms is still unclear but the description of xenopsins (but not c-opsins) in flatworms (Vöcking et al., 2017) suggests CPRs may exist.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Vöcking et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The description of xenopsins in flatworms suggests ciliary photoreceptors may exist in flatworms.
claims.source: The presence and nature of ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms is still unclear but the description of xenopsins (but not c-opsins) in flatworms (Vöcking et al., 2017) suggests CPRs may exist.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of xenopsins.

claims.claim: Ultrastructural studies have identified cells with elaborated ciliary membranes (putative CPRs) in flatworms.
claims.source: Furthermore, ultrastructural studies have identified cells with elaborated ciliary membranes - putative CPRs (Sopott-Ehlers, 1991; Lyons, 1972; Kearn, 1993; Rohde and Watson, 1991) - but these have not been studied at the molecular level.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple ultrastructural studies.

claims.claim: Putative ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms have not been studied at the molecular level.
claims.source: Furthermore, ultrastructural studies have identified cells with elaborated ciliary membranes - putative CPRs (Sopott-Ehlers, 1991; Lyons, 1972; Kearn, 1993; Rohde and Watson, 1991) - but these have not been studied at the molecular level.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: In larvae of the polyclad Pseudoceros canadensis, ultrastructural studies identified three different types of ciliary photoreceptor.
claims.source: In larvae of the polyclad Pseudoceros canadensis, ultrastructural studies identified three different types of CPR; the epidermal eyespot – a pigmented epidermal cell with elaborated ciliary membranes (Lanfranchi et al., 1981; Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); a cerebral eye consisting of a CPR adjacent to RPRs cupped by a supporting pigmented cell (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); and distinct extraocular cells in the epidermis possessing multiple cilia projecting into an intra-cellular vacuole (Lacalli, 1983) known as a phaosome (Fournier, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple ultrastructural studies.

claims.claim: The epidermal eyespot in Pseudoceros canadensis larvae is a pigmented epidermal cell with elaborated ciliary membranes.
claims.source: In larvae of the polyclad Pseudoceros canadensis, ultrastructural studies identified three different types of CPR; the epidermal eyespot – a pigmented epidermal cell with elaborated ciliary membranes (Lanfranchi et al., 1981; Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); a cerebral eye consisting of a CPR adjacent to RPRs cupped by a supporting pigmented cell (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); and distinct extraocular cells in the epidermis possessing multiple cilia projecting into an intra-cellular vacuole (Lacalli, 1983) known as a phaosome (Fournier, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Lanfranchi et al., 1981 and Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981.

claims.claim: A cerebral eye in Pseudoceros canadensis larvae consists of a ciliary photoreceptor adjacent to rhabdomeric photoreceptors cupped by a supporting pigmented cell.
claims.source: In larvae of the polyclad Pseudoceros canadensis, ultrastructural studies identified three different types of CPR; the epidermal eyespot – a pigmented epidermal cell with elaborated ciliary membranes (Lanfranchi et al., 1981; Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); a cerebral eye consisting of a CPR adjacent to RPRs cupped by a supporting pigmented cell (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); and distinct extraocular cells in the epidermis possessing multiple cilia projecting into an intra-cellular vacuole (Lacalli, 1983) known as a phaosome (Fournier, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981.

claims.claim: Distinct extraocular cells in the epidermis of Pseudoceros canadensis larvae possess multiple cilia projecting into an intra-cellular vacuole known as a phaosome.
claims.source: In larvae of the polyclad Pseudoceros canadensis, ultrastructural studies identified three different types of CPR; the epidermal eyespot – a pigmented epidermal cell with elaborated ciliary membranes (Lanfranchi et al., 1981; Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); a cerebral eye consisting of a CPR adjacent to RPRs cupped by a supporting pigmented cell (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981); and distinct extraocular cells in the epidermis possessing multiple cilia projecting into an intra-cellular vacuole (Lacalli, 1983) known as a phaosome (Fournier, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Lacalli, 1983 and Fournier, 1984.

claims.claim: Phaosomal cell type has been found in all classes of flatworm except triclads and bothrioplanids.
claims.source: This phaosomal cell type has been found in all classes of flatworm (except triclads and bothrioplanids) (Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001; Fournier, 1984), and the distinct morphology led to the suggestion that they are a derived feature of flatworms (Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001 and Fournier, 1984.

claims.claim: The distinct morphology of phaosomal cells led to the suggestion that they are a derived feature of flatworms.
claims.source: This phaosomal cell type has been found in all classes of flatworm (except triclads and bothrioplanids) (Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001; Fournier, 1984), and the distinct morphology led to the suggestion that they are a derived feature of flatworms (Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from Sopott-Ehlers et al., 2001.

claims.claim: A 346 amino acid gene product showing similarity to protostome c-opsin and to xenopsin was predicted from a Maritigrella crozieri transcriptome contig.
claims.source: A 346 amino acid gene product showing similarity to protostome c-opsin and to xenopsin was predicted from a Maritigrella crozieri transcriptome contig using BLAST (Madden, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study using BLAST analysis.

claims.claim: Opsins showing similar degrees of similarity to xenopsin were found in transcriptomes from five other flatworm taxa.
claims.source: Opsins showing similar degrees of similarity were found in transcriptomes from five other flatworm taxa (three polyclads; Prostheceraeus vittatus, Stylochus ellipticus, Leptoplana tremellaris and two triclad species Schmidtea mediterranea, Dendrocoelum lacteum).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study using BLAST analysis on transcriptomes.

claims.claim: No homologous xenopsin sequences were found in the remaining 24 flatworm species representing other flatworm classes.
claims.source: We did not find homologous sequences in the remaining 24 flatworm species representing other flatworm classes, including those in which putative CPRs have been described (catenulids, macrostomids, rhabdocoels, proseriates, monogeneans, cestodes and trematodes).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's BLAST searches.

claims.claim: Additional opsins similar to protostome c-opsins and xenopsins were found in a bryozoan, Bugula nerita, and in a chaetognath, Pterosagitta draco.
claims.source: Searching more broadly we found additional opsins similar to protostome c-opsins and xenopsins in a bryozoan, Bugula nerita, and in a chaetognath, Pterosagitta draco.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's broader BLAST searches.

claims.claim: All six polyclad and triclad xenopsin sequences group with clade A of xenopsins.
claims.source: Several polyclad flatworm species show xenopsin paralogs distributed across two xenopsin subgroups (Vöcking et al., 2017); our six polyclad and triclad sequences all group with clade A and we have found xenopsins from three additional taxa to be included in this clade; Maritigrella crozieri, Dendrocoelum lacteum, Leptoplana tremellaris (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Xenopsins are a well-supported monophyletic group of genes most closely related to cnidopsins.
claims.source: The xenopsins are a well-supported monophyletic group of genes most closely related to cnidopsins.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The xenopsin/cnidopsin group is sister to the tetraopsins.
claims.source: The xenopsin/cnidopsin group is sister to the tetraopsins and all are part of a larger clade including bathyopsins and canonical c-opsins (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Support for the relationships between well-defined opsin subtypes is very low.
claims.source: Support for the relationships between these well-defined opsin subtypes is very low, indicating that these relationships should be interpreted cautiously.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the phylogenetic analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Removing smaller opsin clades from the dataset changes the topology of the deeper nodes of the phylogenetic trees.
claims.source: The need for caution is reinforced by the observation that removing the smaller opsin clades from our dataset (chaopsins, bathyopsins, ctenophore and anthozoan opsins), changes the topology of the deeper nodes of our trees (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Flatworm xenopsin protein sequences possess seven transmembrane domains.
claims.source: The flatworm xenopsin protein sequences possess seven transmembrane domains (characteristic of all G protein-coupled receptors) as well as a conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII, which is specific to opsins and which forms a Schiff base with the retinal chromophore to form a photopigment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Flatworm xenopsin protein sequences possess a conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII.
claims.source: The flatworm xenopsin protein sequences possess seven transmembrane domains (characteristic of all G protein-coupled receptors) as well as a conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII, which is specific to opsins and which forms a Schiff base with the retinal chromophore to form a photopigment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII forms a Schiff base with the retinal chromophore to form a photopigment.
claims.source: The flatworm xenopsin protein sequences possess seven transmembrane domains (characteristic of all G protein-coupled receptors) as well as a conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII, which is specific to opsins and which forms a Schiff base with the retinal chromophore to form a photopigment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about opsin function.

claims.claim: Mc xenopsin possesses a tripeptide motif, NxQ, at positions 310–312.
claims.source: Mc xenopsin also possesses a tripeptide motif, NxQ, at positions 310–312, which is reported in other xenopsins (Passamaneck et al., 2011; Vöcking et al., 2017) and in ciliary opsins where it is known to be crucial for G-protein activation (Marin et al., 2000; Gühmann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The NxQ motif is crucial for G-protein activation in ciliary opsins.
claims.source: Mc xenopsin also possesses a tripeptide motif, NxQ, at positions 310–312, which is reported in other xenopsins (Passamaneck et al., 2011; Vöcking et al., 2017) and in ciliary opsins where it is known to be crucial for G-protein activation (Marin et al., 2000; Gühmann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Marin et al., 2000 and Gühmann et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A VxPx motif found in vertebrate ciliary opsins at positions 423–426 is also present in xenopsins.
claims.source: We have found that a second amino acid signature, VxPx, found in vertebrate ciliary opsins at positions 423–426 is also present in xenopsins as well as in ciliary opsin sequences from non-vertebrate chordates (tunicate and lamprey), annelid c-opsins and cnidarian cnidopsins (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: In c-opsins the VxPx motif directly binds the small GTPase Arf4 to direct vertebrate rhodopsin to the primary cilia.
claims.source: In c-opsins this motif directly binds the small GTPase Arf4 to direct vertebrate rhodopsin (a ciliary opsin) to the primary cilia (Deretic et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Deretic et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The presence of the VxPx motif in some ciliary opsins, xenopsins and cnidopsins suggests that Arf4 may be a shared mechanism for the active delivery of these opsins to the cilia in ciliary photoreceptors.
claims.source: The presence of this motif in some ciliary opsins, xenopsins and cnidopsins suggests that Arf4 may be a shared mechanism for the active delivery of these opsins to the cilia in CPRs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of the VxPx motif in multiple opsin types.

claims.claim: A 422 amino acid gene product related to rhabdomeric opsin was predicted from a Maritigrella crozieri transcriptome contig.
claims.source: A 422 amino acid gene product related to rhabdomeric opsin was also predicted from a Maritigrella crozieri transcriptome contig.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study using BLAST analysis.

claims.claim: Nine more flatworm rhabdomeric-like opsins were predicted from both free-living and parasitic species.
claims.source: Nine more flatworm rhabdomeric-like opsins were predicted from both free-living and parasitic species.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's BLAST searches.

claims.claim: Flatworm rhabdomeric-like opsins possess a tripeptide motif (HP[K|R]) following the transmembrane helix VII.
claims.source: They possess a tripeptide motif (HP[K|R]) (supplementary figure 3) following the transmembrane helix VII, which is critical for G-protein binding in r-opsins (Plachetzki and Oakley, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The HP[K|R] motif is critical for G-protein binding in r-opsins.
claims.source: They possess a tripeptide motif (HP[K|R]) (supplementary figure 3) following the transmembrane helix VII, which is critical for G-protein binding in r-opsins (Plachetzki and Oakley, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Plachetzki and Oakley, 2007.

claims.claim: Maritigrella r-opsin and all flatworm r-opsin sequences (except one from Clonorchis sinensis) fall in a monophyletic group containing lophotrochozoan and ecdysozoan r-opsins, and deuterostome melanopsins.

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In the larval stage, xenopsin protein is expressed in the epidermal eye.

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In the larval stage, xenopsin protein is expressed in one of the two cerebral eyes.
claims.source: In the larval stage, xenopsin protein is expressed in the epidermal eye and one of the two cerebral eyes, but not in the epidermal ciliary phaosomes (Figure 2A–C).

claims.claim: In the larval stage, xenopsin protein is not expressed in the epidermal ciliary phaosomes.
claims.source: In the larval stage, xenopsin protein is expressed in the epidermal eye and one of the two cerebral eyes, but not in the epidermal ciliary phaosomes (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: R-opsin mRNA is expressed in both cerebral eyes in the larval stage.
claims.source: R-opsin mRNA is expressed in both cerebral eyes (Figure 2D), but not in the epidermal eye (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: R-opsin mRNA is not expressed in the epidermal eye in the larval stage.
claims.source: R-opsin mRNA is expressed in both cerebral eyes (Figure 2D), but not in the epidermal eye (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: TEM images show that the epidermal eye houses cilia.
claims.source: TEM images show that the epidermal eye and one of the cerebral eyes house cilia (Figure 2E & F), whereas the other cerebral eye contains just microvilli (Figure 2G).

claims.claim: TEM images show that one of the cerebral eyes houses cilia.

claims.claim: The other cerebral eye contains just microvilli.
claims.source: TEM images show that the epidermal eye and one of the cerebral eyes house cilia (Figure 2E & F), whereas the other cerebral eye contains just microvilli (Figure 2G).

claims.claim: In the epidermal eye the cilia are stacked into lamellae.
claims.source: In the epidermal eye the cilia are stacked into lamellae, whereas in the cerebral eye the cilia are unmodified and project into the opticoel.

claims.claim: In the cerebral eye the cilia are unmodified and project into the opticoel.

claims.claim: Xenopsin is co-localised with acetylated tubulin on the cilia of the cerebral eye.

claims.claim: This study shows for the first time xenopsin protein localization to cilia.

claims.claim: The ciliary phaosome cells in the larval epidermis did not express xenopsin.
claims.source: TEM images confirm that the acTub+ cells in the epidermis of Maritigrella larvae (Figure 2B) are cells with multiple cilia projecting into an intracellular vacuole (or phaosome) (Figure 2H); although thought to be CPRs (Lacalli, 1983; Rawlinson, 2010), these cells did not express xenopsin.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The epidermal eye develops before the cerebral eyes in M. crozieri.
claims.source: The epidermal eye develops before the cerebral eyes in M.crozieri (Rawlinson, 2010) and xenopsin is expressed in this eyespot during embryogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Xenopsin is expressed in the epidermal eyespot during embryogenesis.

claims.claim: All pigmented eyes in adult Maritigrella are sub-epidermal and express r-opsin, but not xenopsin.
claims.source: The ontogenetic fates of the epidermal eye and the xenopsin expressing ciliary cell in the cerebral eye are unknown; it could be that both are transient larval features, as all pigmented eyes in adult Maritigrella are sub-epidermal and express r-opsin, but not xenopsin (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Two clusters of up to 100 acTub+ cells were discovered in adult Maritigrella, one either side of the brain.
claims.source: No putative ciliary photoreceptors have been documented in an adult polyclad so, to identify candidates in Maritigrella we first used antibodies against acetylated tubulin and discovered two clusters of up to 100 acTub+ cells, one either side of the brain (Figure 3B,Bi and Di).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella are distributed from the anterior to the posterior of the brain.
claims.source: The cells are distributed from the anterior to the posterior of the brain (Figure 3Di) and extend laterally above nearby branches of the intestine (Figure 3B and Figure 5B).

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella extend laterally above nearby branches of the intestine.
claims.source: The cells are distributed from the anterior to the posterior of the brain (Figure 3Di) and extend laterally above nearby branches of the intestine (Figure 3B and Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B and Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Histological staining showed that the acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella are embedded in extracellular matrix outside of, and lateral to, the brain capsule.
claims.source: Histological staining showed that these cells are embedded in extracellular matrix outside of, and lateral to, the brain capsule (Figure 3C and Ci) and that they sit in close proximity to the main nerve tracts (Figure 3Ci).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data in Figure 3C and Ci.

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella sit in close proximity to the main nerve tracts.
claims.source: Histological staining showed that these cells are embedded in extracellular matrix outside of, and lateral to, the brain capsule (Figure 3C and Ci) and that they sit in close proximity to the main nerve tracts (Figure 3Ci).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data in Figure 3Ci.

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella appear stalked with a nucleus at one end and a balloon-shaped phaosome in the outer segment at the opposite end, which houses multiple cilia.
claims.source: The cells appear stalked with a nucleus at one end and a balloon-shaped phaosome in the outer segment at the opposite end, which houses multiple cilia (Figure 3E,Ei).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E and Ei.

claims.claim: TEM and serial SEM analyzes showed that the acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella house multiple, unmodified cilia in an intra-cellular vacuole.
claims.source: TEM and serial SEM analyzes of these acTub+ cells showed that they house multiple, unmodified cilia in an intra-cellular vacuole and that they sit in close proximity to each other, in dense aggregations (Figure 4A and B, and Figure 4—video 1).

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella sit in close proximity to each other, in dense aggregations.
claims.source: TEM and serial SEM analyzes of these acTub+ cells showed that they house multiple, unmodified cilia in an intra-cellular vacuole and that they sit in close proximity to each other, in dense aggregations (Figure 4A and B, and Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and serial SEM data in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: The acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella are not associated with any pigmented supporting cells.
claims.source: These cells are not associated with any pigmented supporting cells, that is they are extraocular and, although there are unpigmented cells in close proximity (Figure 4), it seems as though the intra-cellular vacuole is completely enclosed by the cell itself and can therefore be considered a phaosome (Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and serial SEM data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The intra-cellular vacuole in the acTub+ cells in adult Maritigrella is completely enclosed by the cell itself and can therefore be considered a phaosome.

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and serial SEM data in Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: The wall of the phaosome cavity in adult Maritigrella is comparatively thin in certain areas (~40 nm).

claims.claim: Each basal body gives rise to one cilium in the phaosome.

claims.claim: The cilia in the phaosome form a tightly intertwined bundle.

claims.claim: The cilia in the phaosome have an average diameter of 0.2 μm and length of 7.2 μm.

claims.source: This represents a total membrane surface area per phaosome of approximately 600 μm2.

claims.claim: The cilia in the phaosome are generally orientated horizontally in relation to the dorso-ventral body axis.

claims.claim: With increasing distance from the base, 9 + 2 singlets are encountered in the axonemata.

claims.claim: No cilia were seen moving in live adult Maritigrella, even in response to changes in illumination.

claims.claim: In the adult, Mc-xenopsin was strongly co-localised with acetylated tubulin in the phaosome cells.

claims.claim: The xenopsin protein was located throughout the cytoplasm of the phaosome cell with strong expression around the base of the cilia.

claims.claim: The xenopsin+ cells sit ventro-lateral to the cerebral eyes.

claims.claim: The cerebral eyes consist of pigmented cup cells and r-opsin+ cells that extend down to the brain.

claims.claim: The pigmented eyes on the tentacles express r-opsin.

claims.claim: The non-overlapping expression of xenopsin and r-opsin indicates that these opsins are expressed in two distinct cell types.

claims.claim: R-opsin-expressing cells also express Gαq.

claims.claim: Mc xenopsin forms a functional photopigment when heterologously expressed in HEK293 cells and reconstituted with 9-cis retinal.

claims.claim: Mc xenopsin elicits a light-dependent decrease in cAMP that is blocked by pertussis toxin when expressed in HEK293 cells.

claims.claim: Mc xenopsin can signal via a Gαi signal transduction cascade.
claims.source: When heterologously expressed in HEK293 cells, and reconstituted with 9-cis retinal, Mc xenopsin elicits a light-dependent decrease in cAMP that is blocked by pertussis toxin, indicating that it can signal via a Gαi signal transduction cascade.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from functional assays shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Mc xenopsin drove a transient increase in intracellular Ca2+ that was blocked by pertussis toxin.

claims.claim: Compared to human rod opsin, Mc xenopsin was effectively irreversibly activated by blue light in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: Compared to human rod opsin, Mc xenopsin was effectively irreversibly activated by blue light in this assay; there was no change in its signaling over tens of minutes.

claims.claim: The prolonged response of Mc xenopsin may reflect an incompatibility with human GPCR kinases and arrestins.

claims.claim: The activated state of Mc xenopsin may be thermally stable and bistable.

claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the prolonged response, citing Tsukamoto and Terakita, 2010.

claims.claim: Bistable opsins, such as lamprey parapinopsin, exhibit prolonged cAMP suppression in response to blue light in live cell assays of Gαi activation.
claims.source: Bistable opsins, such as lamprey parapinopsin, are known to exhibit prolonged cAMP suppression in response to blue light in live cell assays of Gαi activation (Kawano-Yamashita et al., 2015), similar to the responses observed with xenopsin.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Kawano-Yamashita et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Xenopsin's ability to drive phototransduction in live human cell assays and its expression in ciliary cells in Maritigrella add molecular and functional evidence for the presence of ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms.
claims.source: Xenopsin's ability to drive phototransduction in live human cell assays and its expression in ciliary cells in Maritigrella add molecular and functional evidence (albeit indirect) for the presence of ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings and their implications.

claims.claim: Metazoan ciliary photoreceptors are morphologically diverse, especially in the outer segment where the ciliary membranes increase cell surface area.
claims.source: Metazoan ciliary photoreceptors are morphologically diverse, especially in the outer segment where the ciliary membranes increase cell surface area through membrane stacking or greater numbers of cilia, or both.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliary photoreceptor diversity.

claims.claim: In Maritigrella, xenopsin was expressed in three types of ciliary cell each with distinct ciliary arrangements.
claims.source: In Maritigrella, xenopsin was expressed in three types of ciliary cell each with distinct ciliary arrangements; the modified cilia of the larval epidermal eye, the unmodified cilia of the cerebral eye in the larva (which project into extra-cellular space), and the unmodified cilia enclosed in phaosomes in extraocular cells in the adult.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on xenopsin expression.

claims.claim: Xenopsin expression in the ciliary cells of the larval eyes is similar to expression in other larval Lophotrochozoa.
claims.source: Xenopsin expression in the ciliary cells of the larval eyes is similar to expression in other larval Lophotrochozoa; the purely ciliary eye of the brachiopod (Passamaneck et al., 2011), and the mixed ciliary/microvillar, xenopsin and r-opsin expressing eye in a chiton (Vöcking et al., 2017); except that in the chiton xenopsin and r-opsin are co-expressed in a cell that bears both cilia and microvilli, whereas in polyclad larvae the cerebral eye consists of distinct rhabdomeric and ciliary cells (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claims.claim: In the chiton xenopsin and r-opsin are co-expressed in a cell that bears both cilia and microvilli.
claims.source: Xenopsin expression in the ciliary cells of the larval eyes is similar to expression in other larval Lophotrochozoa; the purely ciliary eye of the brachiopod (Passamaneck et al., 2011), and the mixed ciliary/microvillar, xenopsin and r-opsin expressing eye in a chiton (Vöcking et al., 2017); except that in the chiton xenopsin and r-opsin are co-expressed in a cell that bears both cilia and microvilli, whereas in polyclad larvae the cerebral eye consists of distinct rhabdomeric and ciliary cells (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981).

claims.claim: In polyclad larvae the cerebral eye consists of distinct rhabdomeric and ciliary cells.
claims.source: Xenopsin expression in the ciliary cells of the larval eyes is similar to expression in other larval Lophotrochozoa; the purely ciliary eye of the brachiopod (Passamaneck et al., 2011), and the mixed ciliary/microvillar, xenopsin and r-opsin expressing eye in a chiton (Vöcking et al., 2017); except that in the chiton xenopsin and r-opsin are co-expressed in a cell that bears both cilia and microvilli, whereas in polyclad larvae the cerebral eye consists of distinct rhabdomeric and ciliary cells (Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Eakin and Brandenburger, 1981.

claims.claim: The unusual morphology and extraocular location of the xenopsin+ cells in the adult makes them distinct from ciliary photoreceptors in other Metazoa.
claims.source: The unusual morphology, and the extraocular and extra-cerebral location of the xenopsin+ cells in the adult makes them distinct from ciliary photoreceptors in other Metazoa, and only by demonstrating a photoresponse and phototransduction in these cells in the live worms would we have direct evidence that they are ciliary photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the distinctiveness of the xenopsin+ cells.

claims.claim: Maritigrella ciliary phaosomes are 'rod-like' because they enclose their ciliary membranes within their own plasma membrane.
claims.source: Firstly, while most metazoan CPRs project their ciliary membranes outside of the cell (like jawed vertebrate cones), Maritigrella ciliary phaosomes are more 'rod-like' because they enclose their ciliary membranes within their own plasma membrane, like gnathostome rods and a few examples of ciliary phaosomes from other invertebrates (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with vertebrate rods based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Maritigrella phaosome cells increase their surface area by increasing the number of cilia rather than modifying the ciliary membranes into discs or lamellae.
claims.source: Secondly, Maritigrella phaosome cells increase their surface area by increasing the number of cilia rather than modifying the ciliary membranes into discs or lamellae (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's ultrastructural analysis.

claims.claim: The sheer number of cilia housed within the phaosome may be a unique feature of Maritigrella and other flatworm ciliary photoreceptors.
claims.source: The sheer number of cilia housed within the phaosome is striking and may be a unique feature of Maritigrella and other flatworm CPRs.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and comparison with other organisms.

claims.claim: A few examples of unmodified cilia in complete or open phaosomes have been recorded in other lophotrochozoans.
claims.source: A few examples of unmodified cilia in complete or open phaosomes have been recorded in other lophotrochozoans (Hessling and Purschke, 2000; Woollacott and Zimmer, 1972), but most other phaosomal CPRs have modified cilia (flattened and whorled) (Clement and Wurdak, 1984; Boyle, 1969; Horridge, 1964).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claims.claim: Most other phaosomal ciliary photoreceptors have modified cilia (flattened and whorled).
claims.source: A few examples of unmodified cilia in complete or open phaosomes have been recorded in other lophotrochozoans (Hessling and Purschke, 2000; Woollacott and Zimmer, 1972), but most other phaosomal CPRs have modified cilia (flattened and whorled) (Clement and Wurdak, 1984; Boyle, 1969; Horridge, 1964).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claims.claim: The patchy phylogenetic distribution of cells that enclose their ciliary processes suggests this trait has evolved independently in these taxa.
claims.source: The patchy phylogenetic distribution of cells that enclose their ciliary processes suggests this trait has evolved independently in these taxa (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In the Clitellata, microvillar, r-opsin-expressing phaosomes are the only type of photoreceptor found.
claims.source: Phaosomes are not specific to ciliary photoreceptors, in the Clitellata, a major annelid group, microvillar, r-opsin-expressing phaosomes are the only type of photoreceptor found (Döring et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Döring et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Rods evolved from cones to give highly sensitive but coarse monochromatic scotopic vision at night.
claims.source: Rods evolved from cones (Kawamura and Tachibanaki, 2008; Morshedian and Fain, 2015) to give highly sensitive but coarse monochromatic scotopic vision at night.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Kawamura and Tachibanaki, 2008 and Morshedian and Fain, 2015.

claims.claim: The defining feature of a rod is its ability to respond to single photons of light in the dark-adapted state.
claims.source: Physiologically, the defining feature of a rod is its ability to respond to single photons of light in the dark-adapted state (Baylor et al., 1979).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Baylor et al., 1979.

claims.claim: The high sensitivity of rods is further enhanced by very slow response kinetics, slow transduction machinery and a slow recovery of visual sensitivity following bleaching, compared to cones.
claims.source: This high sensitivity of rods is further enhanced by very slow response kinetics, slow transduction machinery and a slow recovery of visual sensitivity following bleaching, compared to cones (summarized in Warrant 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge summarized in Warrant 2015.

claims.claim: The phaosomal cells of Maritigrella adults are not associated with pigment cup cells and are therefore extraocular.
claims.source: Our morphological analyzes show that the phaosomal cells of Maritigrella adults are not associated with pigment cup cells, they are therefore extraocular and could detect light from all directions.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's morphological analysis.

claims.claim: The phaosomal cells of Maritigrella adults could detect light from all directions.
claims.source: Our morphological analyzes show that the phaosomal cells of Maritigrella adults are not associated with pigment cup cells, they are therefore extraocular and could detect light from all directions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the extraocular location of the cells.

claims.claim: The density of phaosome cells in Maritigrella, and the number of cilia in each phaosome, increases the surface area to allow higher concentrations of photopigment, which would suggest very high sensitivity to light.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological findings.

claims.claim: The ciliary surface area of a phaosome is two times larger than that of the brain ciliary photoreceptors of the annelid Platynereis.
claims.source: The ciliary surface area of a phaosome is approximately four times smaller than the total disc membrane surface of rat rods (Mayhew and Astle, 1997) but two times larger than that of the brain CPRs of the annelid Platynereis (Verasztó et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on calculations from the study's data and cited literature.

claims.claim: The adult xenopsin+ ciliary phaosomes of Maritigrella are extraocular like the ciliary photoreceptors of the marine annelid Platynereis.
claims.source: The adult xenopsin+ ciliary phaosomes of Maritigrella are extraocular like the CPRs of the marine annelid Platynereis. In the annelid these are located in the brain and express a UV-sensitive ciliary opsin (Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with established knowledge cited from Arendt et al., 2004 and Tsukamoto et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In the annelid Platynereis, extraocular ciliary photoreceptors are located in the brain and express a UV-sensitive ciliary opsin.
claims.source: The adult xenopsin+ ciliary phaosomes of Maritigrella are extraocular like the CPRs of the marine annelid Platynereis. In the annelid these are located in the brain and express a UV-sensitive ciliary opsin (Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Arendt et al., 2004 and Tsukamoto et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The extraocular ciliary photoreceptors in Platynereis control circadian behaviors via melatonin production.

claims.claim: The extraocular ciliary photoreceptors in Platynereis mediate downward swimming in response to non-directional UV light in the larval stage.

claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Verasztó et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The Platynereis c-opsin binds to exogenous all-trans-retinal.
claims.source: The Platynereis c-opsin binds to exogenous all-trans-retinal, which is particularly important for opsins expressed outside of the eyes (Tsukamoto et al., 2017) where sophisticated multi-enzyme systems producing a thermally unstable 11-cis-retinal isomer probably don't exist (Yau and Hardie, 2009).

claims.claim: Binding to exogenous all-trans-retinal is particularly important for opsins expressed outside of the eyes.
claims.source: The Platynereis c-opsin binds to exogenous all-trans-retinal, which is particularly important for opsins expressed outside of the eyes (Tsukamoto et al., 2017) where sophisticated multi-enzyme systems producing a thermally unstable 11-cis-retinal isomer probably don't exist (Yau and Hardie, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Tsukamoto et al., 2017 and Yau and Hardie, 2009.

claims.claim: The discovery of xenopsin+ ciliary cells in the eyes of protostome larvae challenged views on opsin and photoreceptor evolution by deviating from the invertebrate trend of extraocular ciliary photoreceptors and ocular rhabdomeric/microvillar photoreceptors.
claims.source: The discovery of xenopsin+ ciliary cells in the eyes of protostome larvae challenged our views on opsin and photoreceptor evolution by deviating from the invertebrate trend of extraocular ciliary photoreceptors and ocular rhabdomeric/microvillar photoreceptors (Passamaneck et al., 2011; Vöcking et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Xenopsin expression is both ocular and extraocular, either simultaneously or sequentially over development.
claims.source: Xenopsin expression is both ocular and extraocular, however, either simultaneously (e.g. in the chiton larva [Vöcking et al., 2017]) or sequentially over development as we have shown in Maritigrella (e.g. in the larval eyes and adult extraocular ciliary phaosomes), and this is a feature of most opsin types (Porter et al., 2012; Cronin and Porter, 2014; Sprecher and Desplan, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings and comparison with other opsins.

claims.claim: Ocular and extraocular expression is a feature of most opsin types.
claims.source: Xenopsin expression is both ocular and extraocular, however, either simultaneously (e.g. in the chiton larva [Vöcking et al., 2017]) or sequentially over development as we have shown in Maritigrella (e.g. in the larval eyes and adult extraocular ciliary phaosomes), and this is a feature of most opsin types (Porter et al., 2012; Cronin and Porter, 2014; Sprecher and Desplan, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claims.claim: The findings show that xenopsin is localized in different types of ciliary cell, with different functions (ocular and extraocular) at different points in development.
claims.source: Our findings show that xenopsin is localized in different types of cillary cell, with different functions (ocular and extraocular) at different points in development, highlighting the importance of including developmental data into evolutionary scenarios on photoreceptor evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Xenopsin in the extra-ocular ciliary phaosomes of adult Maritigrella is consistent with the invertebrate trend of extra-ocular ciliary photoreceptors.
claims.source: In fact, xenopsin in the extra-ocular ciliary phaosomes of adult Maritigrella is yet another similarity with ciliary opsin (which is expressed in extra-ocular CPRs of annelids and arthropods) and is consistent with the invertebrate trend of extra-ocular ciliary photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and comparison with other organisms.

claims.claim: Phylogenetic reconstructions of opsin gene family relationships support the emerging consensus that xenopsins and c-opsins diverged prior to the bilaterian common ancestor.

claims.claim: Both xenopsins and c-opsins co-existed in the protostome stem lineage.
claims.source: As both opsin types are found in various protostomes, this suggests that the two opsins co-existed in the protostome stem lineage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution.

claims.claim: No species is known in which both xenopsins and c-opsins are present.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: The survey of flatworm opsins revealed another instance in which only one of the two related xenopsin/c-opsins types is found.
claims.source: Our survey of flatworm opsins has revealed another instance in which only one of the two related xenopsin/c-opsins types is found.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's survey of flatworm opsins.

claims.claim: The same pattern of having only one of xenopsin or c-opsin is true of a chaetognath and a bryozoan.
claims.source: We find that the same is true of a chaetognath and a bryozoan.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's survey of opsins.

claims.claim: One possibility to explain the distribution of xenopsins and c-opsins is that the two opsins are largely equivalent despite being clearly separate clades.
claims.source: One possibility to explain this distribution is that, while clearly separate clades with distinct and conserved genes structures unique to each type of opsin, the two opsins are, nevertheless, largely equivalent.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional equivalence of xenopsins and c-opsins.

claims.claim: The study provided two pieces of evidence that suggest Gαi coupling of xenopsin: primary activation of a Gαi signal transduction cascade in living human cells, and xenopsin and Gαi localization in the same putative ciliary photoreceptor in a flatworm.
claims.source: Going beyond comparative analysis of amino acid sequences, we have provided two pieces of evidence that suggest Gαi coupling of xenopsin; primary activation of a Gαi signal transduction cascade in living human cells, and xenopsin and Gαi localization in the same putative ciliary photoreceptor in a flatworm.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on Gαi coupling.

claims.claim: The study showed xenopsin protein expression on cilia of cells that form eyes, supporting the possibility that the VxPx motif is also involved in transporting xenopsin to cilia.

results.result: Xenopsin and rhabdomeric opsin sequences were identified in flatworms and other taxa through phylogenetic analysis. Flatworm xenopsins group with clade A and form a monophyletic group most closely related to cnidopsins. The xenopsin sequences possess characteristic opsin features including seven transmembrane domains, a conserved lysine in transmembrane domain VII, and the NxQ and VxPx motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C59 describe sequence identification and phylogenetic placement supported by BLAST searches (C38-C41), phylogenetic trees shown in Figure 1 (C42-C44), and sequence analysis (C47-C48, C50, C52). The phylogenetic analysis appropriately uses multiple methods (IQ-TREE and RAxML) with bootstrap support values. The authors appropriately note low support for deeper relationships (C45-C46), demonstrating critical assessment of their own results.

results.result: In larval Maritigrella, xenopsin is expressed in the epidermal eye and one cerebral eye (which contain cilia), but not in epidermal ciliary phaosomes. R-opsin is expressed in both cerebral eyes but not the epidermal eye. This represents the first demonstration of xenopsin protein localization to cilia.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C73 describe larval opsin expression patterns supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 2A-C), in situ hybridization (Figure 2D), and TEM (Figure 2E-H). The co-localization of xenopsin with acetylated tubulin on cilia (C70) provides direct evidence for ciliary localization. The complementary expression patterns of xenopsin and r-opsin are well-documented with appropriate controls and multiple imaging modalities.

results.result: Adult Maritigrella possess clusters of ~100 acetylated tubulin-positive cells near the brain that contain phaosomes housing at least 421 unmodified cilia in intracellular vacuoles. These extraocular cells have unique ultrastructural features including a thin cavity wall (~40 nm), mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, and cilia with varying microtubule arrangements (9×2+2 to singlets). The cilia appear non-motile based on absence of rootlets and lack of observed movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C104 describe the morphology of adult phaosome cells supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 3), TEM and serial SEM (Figure 4). The quantification of ciliary number (C92) is based on direct counting from serial SEM. The ultrastructural characterization is thorough with appropriate measurements and 3D reconstructions. The inference about non-motility (C102) is appropriately cautious given the observation of possible dynein arms (C103) and lack of movement in live animals (C104).

results.result: In adult Maritigrella, xenopsin is strongly co-localized with acetylated tubulin in phaosome cells, with expression throughout the cytoplasm and strong expression around ciliary bases. R-opsin is expressed in cerebral and tentacular eyes along with Gαq, while Gαi is expressed in phaosome cells including on ciliary membranes. The non-overlapping expression patterns indicate distinct cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C114 describe adult opsin and G-protein expression supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 5A-E, H-J) and in situ hybridization (Figure 5F). The co-localization studies use appropriate markers (acetylated tubulin for cilia, DAPI for nuclei). The identification of Gα subunits in the transcriptome (C112-C113) provides context, though the antibody-based localization has limitations acknowledged by the authors (only Gαi and Gαq showed specific localization).

results.result: Maritigrella xenopsin forms a functional photopigment in HEK293 cells that primarily couples to Gαi, causing light-dependent cAMP suppression blocked by pertussis toxin. The Ca2+ response is also pertussis toxin-sensitive, indicating crosstalk with Gαi rather than Gαq coupling. Xenopsin shows promiscuous signaling to Gαs when Gαi is blocked, and exhibits prolonged activation compared to human rod opsin.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C122 describe functional characterization supported by live-cell assays in Figure 6. The experiments appropriately use pertussis toxin to distinguish Gαi-mediated effects, include positive controls (JellyOp for Gαs, rod opsin for Gαi, melanopsin for Gαq), and show three biological replicates (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The interpretation that Ca2+ response reflects Gαi crosstalk rather than Gαq coupling (C119) is well-supported by pertussis toxin sensitivity. The prolonged activation (C122) is clearly demonstrated but mechanistic interpretation remains speculative.

results.result: Xenopsin is expressed in ciliary cells of larval eyes and in extraocular cells around the adult brain that house hundreds of cilia in phaosomes. Functional assays show xenopsin drives phototransduction primarily through Gαi coupling. These cells enclose ciliary membranes within their plasma membrane, similar to vertebrate rods.
results.evaluation: This summary result integrates the major findings from the abstract (C3-C7) which are supported by the detailed experimental results described in other claim groups. The expression patterns are documented by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization, the ultrastructure by TEM/SEM, and the Gαi coupling by functional assays. The comparison to vertebrate rods (C7) is supported by the ultrastructural data showing enclosed ciliary membranes.

results.result: The NxQ motif is crucial for G-protein activation in ciliary opsins, and the VxPx motif binds Arf4 to direct rhodopsin to primary cilia. The presence of these motifs in xenopsins suggests shared mechanisms for G-protein activation and ciliary targeting.
results.evaluation: Claims C51 and C53 cite established knowledge about motif function in ciliary opsins. Claim C54 is an inference about xenopsin function based on sequence similarity. While the inference is reasonable given the sequence conservation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, direct experimental validation of Arf4 binding or ciliary targeting mechanism for xenopsin is not provided. The inference is appropriately presented as a suggestion rather than a definitive conclusion.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis supports that xenopsins and c-opsins diverged before the bilaterian common ancestor and co-existed in the protostome stem lineage. However, no species is known with both opsin types present, suggesting they may be functionally equivalent despite being distinct clades.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C163 describe phylogenetic findings and taxonomic distribution patterns supported by Figure 1 and the survey of flatworm opsins (C162-C163). The speculation about functional equivalence (C164) is appropriately presented as one possibility to explain the mutually exclusive distribution. The phylogenetic support for deep relationships is acknowledged as low (C45), appropriately tempering conclusions about ancient divergence.

results.result: The study provides evidence for Gαi coupling of xenopsin through functional assays in human cells and co-localization with Gαi in flatworm phaosome cells. Xenopsin protein expression on cilia supports the role of the VxPx motif in ciliary targeting. Conserved sequence motifs lead to similar function (Gαi binding) and expression (ciliary cells) between xenopsin and c-opsin.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 summarize key functional findings supported by the HEK293 assays (Figure 6) and immunolocalization studies (Figures 2, 5). The evidence for Gαi coupling is strong from the functional assays. The ciliary localization is well-documented. However, the direct role of the VxPx motif in xenopsin ciliary targeting (C166) remains inferential based on sequence similarity rather than direct experimental manipulation.

results.result: Xenopsins duplicated into two clades (A and B). Clade A xenopsins have signatures of photopigments including the NxQ and VxPx motifs, while clade B xenopsins lack these motifs despite having the chromophore-binding lysine. Clade B xenopsins might function as photoisomerases.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 describe sequence differences between xenopsin clades supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1) and sequence alignments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). However, the speculation that clade B xenopsins are photoisomerases (C171) lacks experimental support. This is appropriately presented as speculation, but no functional data on clade B xenopsins is provided. The hypothesis is reasonable but remains untested.

results.result: The prolonged response of Mc xenopsin may reflect incompatibility with human GPCR kinases and arrestins, or the activated state may be thermally stable and bistable. Bistable opsins like lamprey parapinopsin show similar prolonged cAMP suppression.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 documents the prolonged activation with data from Figure 6B. Claims C123-C124 present two possible explanations but are explicitly speculative. The comparison to bistable opsins (C125) cites relevant literature but does not provide direct evidence that xenopsin is bistable. Distinguishing between these mechanisms would require additional experiments (e.g., testing for photoreversal, measuring thermal stability of the activated state). The speculation is reasonable but the mechanism remains unresolved.

results.result: Xenopsin expression in ciliary cells and ability to drive phototransduction provide evidence for ciliary photoreceptors in flatworms. The xenopsin-expressing cells have unusual morphology with three distinct ciliary arrangements across development. Adult phaosome cells are 'rod-like' in enclosing ciliary membranes and increase surface area through ciliary number rather than membrane modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C128, C132-C135 synthesize morphological and functional findings. The evidence for ciliary photoreceptor function is indirect (C126 acknowledges this) but substantial, combining opsin expression, ciliary localization, Gαi co-expression, and functional phototransduction. The morphological characterization (C133-C134) is well-supported by TEM/SEM data. The speculation about uniqueness (C135) is appropriately cautious. Direct demonstration of photoresponse in native cells would strengthen the conclusion but is technically challenging.

results.result: Adult phaosome cells are extraocular and could detect light from all directions. The high density of cells and cilia suggests high light sensitivity. The ciliary surface area per phaosome (~600 μm²) is smaller than rat rods but larger than Platynereis brain ciliary photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is supported by the absence of pigment cup cells in TEM/SEM data. The inference about omnidirectional light detection (C144) is reasonable given the extraocular location. The suggestion of high sensitivity (C145) is logical based on membrane surface area but remains inferential without physiological measurements. The surface area calculations (C146-C147) are based on measurements from the study and cited literature, providing useful comparative context.

results.result: Xenopsin expression is both ocular and extraocular, either simultaneously or sequentially over development, which is a feature of most opsin types. The findings highlight the importance of developmental data for understanding photoreceptor evolution. Xenopsin in extraocular phaosomes is consistent with the invertebrate trend of extraocular ciliary photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C158 place the findings in evolutionary context. The developmental shift in xenopsin expression (C155, C157) is documented by comparing larval (Figure 2) and adult (Figure 5) expression patterns. The comparison to other opsins (C156) cites appropriate literature. The consistency with invertebrate trends (C158) is a reasonable inference. These claims appropriately integrate the study's findings with broader understanding of opsin evolution.

results.result: Background knowledge about photoreceptor types, opsin families, xenopsin distribution, flatworm photoreceptors, and comparisons to other organisms.
